cultivar: Seed-grown bushes of Chinese origin planted in the nineteenth century
processing: The leaf is heated to stop oxidation shortly after picking, then rolled on the estate's old machinery and dried; it is a simple, unshaded, fairly robust green tea made on equipment designed for black tea.
harvest_season: April to September, from the same bushes as the black grades; the spring leaf gives the softest green.
appearance_dry: Dark olive, loosely twisted leaves of mixed size with some stems and a hay-like smell.
appearance_wet: Olive-green leaves, medium size, fairly tough.
taste_profile: Plain, grassy and slightly astringent with hay, a faint mineral-saline edge and a short, clean finish; a straightforward green tea rather than a delicate one, and very good iced.

brewing.notes: Cooled water and a short steep tame its astringency; it is more forgiving than a Japanese green and makes a clean cold brew. On the island it is often served iced with lemon.

vintage_note: Sold year-round under the names Hysson, Encosta de Bruma and Pérola in boxes and tins from the estate, blended across the season and not dated; buy the freshest box you can, keep it sealed, and drink it within the year, as with any green tea.
description:
Gorreana's green tea is the lesser-known half of Europe's oldest tea estate, made on the same north coast of São Miguel from the same century-old Chinese-origin bushes as its black grades. The estate sells it under the old trade name Hysson, a word that in the nineteenth century meant a Chinese green tea grade and that survives here as a label.

It is made simply: the leaf is heated soon after picking to stop oxidation, rolled on the estate's veteran machinery and dried. There is no shading, no steaming in the Japanese sense and no pan-fired artistry; this is a green tea made in a black-tea factory, and it tastes that way, robust and plain rather than fine. The Atlantic climate and the absence of pesticides are the same as for the black.

The cup is grassy and a little astringent, with hay, a faint saline-mineral note and a short clean finish. Brewed with cooled water and a short steep it is a pleasant everyday green; brewed with boiling water it turns bitter quickly. Where it shines is cold, and the Azoreans drink it iced with lemon through the summer.

It is sold year-round, without a date, as Hysson and two other green teas, Encosta de Bruma and Pérola, from the estate shop, Portuguese groceries and online, at a modest price. Expect a rustic European green tea rather than a rival to a good Chinese or Japanese one, and it will not disappoint.

Taste it next to the estate's Orange Pekoe to see the same leaf oxidised and not; and if you like soft, rustic greens, the Georgian and Krasnodar greens from the Black Sea are the other European examples worth trying.
sources_note: The exact method by which Gorreana fixes its green tea (steam versus dry heat) is not stated precisely by the estate in sources I trust, so the card says only 'heated'. 'Hysson' as the estate's green grade name is from its own product range.
history:
Gorreana, on the north coast of São Miguel in the Azores, makes green tea alongside its better-known blacks. Its green range includes Hysson, Encosta de Bruma and Pérola, and as of 2021 the estate's whole output, black and green together, was 30 to 40 tons a year.

The tea is grown without pesticides, which is credited to a relatively dry climate and isolation from parasites. Exactly how the leaf is fixed is not clearly documented.
